items.title: Large inversions in Lake Malawi cichlids are associated with habitat, lineage, and sex determination
items.why: A peer-reviewed eLife study using optical mapping, PacBio HiFi assemblies and short-read genotyping to characterize six large inversions in Lake Malawi cichlids. It adds an evolutionary-genetics topic outside the usual AI/molecular feed. The inversion-to-sex-determination link is described as limited to a subset of species.
items.takeaway: The inversions largely segregate by ecogroup, and the authors propose that three spread into benthic lineages by hybridization.

items.title: Lessons in Bemistry: identifying the signature of a medicinal chemist
items.why: A short blog post on a preprint showing that a model can infer which medicinal chemist made a molecule from its structure. That makes it a Clever Hans warning for activity-prediction benchmarks. The post itself flags that top-k accuracy rather than balanced accuracy may be inflating the result.
items.takeaway: Author-probability vectors plus a protein ID reportedly rival an ECFP4 baseline, but the reported accuracy may reflect a few easy authors.

items.title: Visual Information Theory
items.why: A visual, from-first-principles explanation of probability factorization, Simpson's paradox, codes and entropy.
items.takeaway: Entropy is the limit on average code length, and short codewords for common events cost space in the codeword budget.

items.title: Generative modelling in latent space
items.why: Explains the two-stage latent recipe (autoencoder, then generative model) behind most modern image, audio and video generators, and why it became standard. It is useful background for generative modelling of scientific data.
items.takeaway: The first stage uses reconstruction, perceptual and adversarial losses. The generative model is then trained on frozen latents.

items.title: AlphaFold2 @ CASP14: “It feels like one’s child has left home.”
items.why: A domain expert's account of what AlphaFold2 at CASP14 did and did not show. It covers the GDT_TS metric, the meaning of 'solved', and what is unknown about the method. It is an opinionated blog post, not the primary paper, and was written when method details were thin.
items.takeaway: The post is cautious that AF2 predicts structures trained on crystallographic data, not necessarily lowest-energy states.

items.title: A Recipe for Cells
items.why: An essay on what a bacterial cell is made of and what it costs to build one. It covers molecular composition, noisy expression and fault tolerance, which gives context for any modelling of cells. It is essay-style synthesis, so check the original papers for the numbers.
items.takeaway: Even genetically identical E. coli vary substantially in gene expression, and cell survival depends partly on population-level fault tolerance.

items.title: Adversarial Reprogramming of Neural Cellular Automata
items.why: A Distill article on adversarially reprogramming neural cellular automata. It is an unfamiliar intersection of self-organization, robustness and biological signaling, and the authors note which attacks worked poorly.
items.takeaway: A small fraction of adversarial cells can hijack pretrained digit-classifying cells. Reprogramming the growing lizard pattern was harder and less reliable.

items.title: Scaling Laws, Carefully
items.why: A careful review of scaling-law methodology: the Kaplan versus Chinchilla compute-optimal allocations, three fitting methods, and the pitfalls of fitting. It supports rigorous evaluation and optimization thinking.
items.takeaway: Kaplan et al. and Chinchilla disagree on how to split compute between model size and data, and the post covers how to reconcile them.

items.title: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out.
items.why: A code-along video that builds a GPT from scratch. It is a hands-on way to understand transformer language models. The length is my estimate, since the supplied excerpt shows only the title.
items.takeaway: The title says it builds GPT from scratch, in code.

earlier.title: Identifying Interactions at Scale for LLMs
earlier.why: Introduces SPEX and ProxySPEX, methods that find interactions among features, training points or attention heads using relatively few ablations. It is relevant to interpretability and attribution in scientific models. The results are the authors' own, and open code is in the SHAP-IQ repository.
earlier.takeaway: The authors report that ProxySPEX matches SPEX with about 10x fewer ablations by exploiting hierarchy among interactions.
